claim: The fruit fly can evaluate its energy state and decide whether to pursue food-related cues.
source: The fruit fly can evaluate its energy state and decide whether to pursue food-related cues.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract introducing the study's context.

claim: The mushroom body (MB) integrates hunger and satiety signals to control food-seeking behavior.
source: Here, we reveal that the mushroom body (MB) integrates hunger and satiety signals to control food-seeking behavior.
evidence: This is the main finding of the study as stated in the abstract.

claim: Five pathways in the MB are essential for hungry flies to locate and approach food.
source: We have discovered five pathways in the MB essential for hungry flies to locate and approach food.
evidence: This claim is supported by the behavioral experiments described in the manuscript.

claim: Blocking the MB-intrinsic Kenyon cells (KCs) impairs food-seeking behavior.
source: Blocking the MB-intrinsic Kenyon cells (KCs) and the MB output neurons (MBONs) in these pathways impairs food-seeking behavior.
evidence: This is supported by experiments using UAS-shits1 to block KC neurotransmission.

claim: Blocking the MB output neurons (MBONs) in these pathways impairs food-seeking behavior.
source: Blocking the MB-intrinsic Kenyon cells (KCs) and the MB output neurons (MBONs) in these pathways impairs food-seeking behavior.
evidence: This is supported by experiments using UAS-shits1 to block MBON neurotransmission.

claim: Starvation bi-directionally modulates MBON responses to a food odor.
source: Starvation bi-directionally modulates MBON responses to a food odor, suggesting that hunger and satiety controls occur at the KC-to-MBON synapses.
evidence: This is supported by in vivo calcium imaging experiments showing both increases and decreases in MBON responses to yeast odor depending on the MBON type.

claim: Hunger and satiety controls occur at the KC-to-MBON synapses.
source: Starvation bi-directionally modulates MBON responses to a food odor, suggesting that hunger and satiety controls occur at the KC-to-MBON synapses.
evidence: This is inferred from the bi-directional modulation of MBON responses and the lack of changes in KC responses to yeast odor.

claim: Six types of dopaminergic neurons (DANs) mediate the hunger and satiety controls.
source: These controls are mediated by six types of dopaminergic neurons (DANs).
evidence: This is supported by experiments blocking and activating specific DANs.

claim: Manipulating DANs can inhibit food-seeking behavior in hungry flies.
source: By manipulating these DANs, we could inhibit food-seeking behavior in hungry flies or promote food seeking in fed flies.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experiments using UAS-TrpA1 and UAS-shits1 to activate or block DANs.

claim: Manipulating DANs can promote food seeking in fed flies.
source: By manipulating these DANs, we could inhibit food-seeking behavior in hungry flies or promote food seeking in fed flies.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experiments using UAS-TrpA1 and UAS-shits1 to activate or block DANs.

claim: The DANs potentially receive multiple inputs of hunger and satiety signals.
source: Finally, we show that the DANs potentially receive multiple inputs of hunger and satiety signals.
evidence: This is supported by RNAi knockdown experiments of various receptors in DANs.

claim: The MB is an information-rich central circuit in the fly brain that controls hunger-driven food-seeking behavior.
source: This work demonstrates an information-rich central circuit in the fly brain that controls hunger-driven food-seeking behavior.
evidence: This is the overall conclusion of the study based on all the experimental findings.

claim: The main nutrient- and energy-sensing organs in vertebrates are stomach, gut, and white adipose tissue.
source: The main nutrient- and energy-sensing organs in vertebrates are stomach, gut, and white adipose tissue (Kairupan et al., 2016; Porte et al., 2002; Small and Bloom, 2004).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: Hormones such as leptin, ghrelin, neuropeptide Y (NPY), and cholecystokinin serve as hunger and satiety signals in the nervous system.
source: Hormones such as leptin, ghrelin, neuropeptide Y (NPY), and cholecystokinin that are secreted by these organs serve as hunger and satiety signals in the nervous system and control how an animal responds to food cues (Kairupan et al., 2016; Porte et al., 2002; Sternson et al., 2013; Sternson and Eiselt, 2017).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: Hormonal signals play important roles in mediating hunger control in Drosophila.
source: Hormonal signals also play important roles in mediating hunger control in the fruit fly Drosophila; these include insulin-like peptides, the two homologs of mammalian NPY (Neuropeptide F, NPF, and short Neuropeptide F, sNPF), the homolog of mammalian leptin (Unpaired 2, Upd2), the insect analog of glucagon (adipokinetic hormone, AKH), and a handful of other neuropeptides and metabolites (Dus et al., 2015; Inagaki et al., 2014; Jourjine et al., 2016; Kim et al., 2017; Lee et al., 2004; Pool and Scott, 2014; Rajan and Perrimon, 2012; Root et al., 2011; Sun et al., 2017; Wu et al., 2005; Yu et al., 2016).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: Flies primarily rely on olfactory cues to locate food.
source: Flies primarily rely on olfactory cues to locate food.
evidence: This is a general statement based on established knowledge about fly behavior.

claim: Starvation sensitizes the olfactory receptor neurons (ORNs) for attractive odors via the cooperation of insulin and sNPF signaling pathways.
source: Starvation sensitizes the olfactory receptor neurons (ORNs) for attractive odors via the cooperation of insulin and sNPF signaling pathways (Root et al., 2011) and, in parallel, dampens the activity of ORNs for aversive odors through the neuropeptide tachykinin released from interneurons in the antennal lobe (Ko et al., 2015).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: Starvation dampens the activity of ORNs for aversive odors through the neuropeptide tachykinin released from interneurons in the antennal lobe.
source: Starvation sensitizes the olfactory receptor neurons (ORNs) for attractive odors via the cooperation of insulin and sNPF signaling pathways (Root et al., 2011) and, in parallel, dampens the activity of ORNs for aversive odors through the neuropeptide tachykinin released from interneurons in the antennal lobe (Ko et al., 2015).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: The neuropeptide CCHamide is involved in hunger-induced modulation in ORNs.
source: Another neuropeptide, CCHamide, is also involved in hunger-induced modulation in ORNs (Farhan et al., 2013).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: A pair of NPF-expressing neurons in the adult brain encode odor attractiveness.
source: A pair of NPF-expressing neurons in the adult brain have been shown to encode odor attractiveness (Beshel and Zhong, 2013).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: Starvation heightens the activity of the NPF neurons.
source: Importantly, starvation heightens the activity of the NPF neurons, but how the graded NPF signal is translated into approach behavior is not known.
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: Food odors detected by specific ORNs are relayed by antennal lobe projection neurons to the mushroom body (MB) and lateral horn (LH).
source: Food odors detected by specific ORNs are relayed by antennal lobe projection neurons to the mushroom body (MB) and lateral horn (LH) (Jefferis et al., 2007; Lin et al., 2007; Stocker et al., 1997).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: The LH plays a major role in innate olfactory behavior.
source: It has been suggested that the LH plays a major role in innate olfactory behavior (de Belle and Heisenberg, 1994; Heimbeck et al., 2001; Jefferis et al., 2007; Parnas et al., 2013; Strutz et al., 2014).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: Neural modulation in the LH has been shown to regulate feeding behavior in Drosophila larvae.
source: Neural modulation in the LH has been shown to regulate feeding behavior in Drosophila larvae.
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: Brief presentation of appetizing odors causes voracious feeding on sugar-rich food even in fed larvae; a process involving NPF neurons and dopaminergic neurons projecting to the LH.
source: Brief presentation of appetizing odors causes voracious feeding on sugar-rich food even in fed larvae; a process involving NPF neurons and dopaminergic neurons projecting to the LH (Wang et al., 2013).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: The MB is conventionally considered to be an olfactory learning and memory center.
source: In contrast to the LH, the MB is conventionally considered to be an olfactory learning and memory center (de Belle and Heisenberg, 1994; Heisenberg, 2003; Keene and Waddell, 2007; McGuire et al., 2005).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: The MB is composed of around 2200 intrinsic neurons called Kenyon Cells (KC).
source: The MB is composed of around 2200 intrinsic neurons called Kenyon Cells (KC), which extend parallel axonal fibers to form the γ, α′β′, and αβ lobes of the MB (Aso et al., 2014a; Crittenden et al., 1998; Lin et al., 2007; Strausfeld et al., 2003; Tanaka et al., 2008).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: Each KC receives inputs from a random combination of antennal lobe projection neurons.
source: Each KC receives inputs from a random combination of antennal lobe projection neurons (Caron et al., 2013).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: The KC outputs converge onto 21 types of 34 MB output neurons (MBONs).
source: The KC outputs converge onto 21 types of 34 MB output neurons (MBONs).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: The dendrites of each MBON type arborize in specific compartments of the MB lobes.
source: The dendrites of each MBON type arborize in specific compartments of the MB lobes, and all MBON types together innervate 15 distinct compartments that tile the MB lobes (Aso et al., 2014a).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: About 130 MB-innervating DANs of 20 cell types have been identified.
source: About 130 MB-innervating DANs of 20 cell types have been identified (Aso et al., 2014a).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: Distinct types of DANs react selectively to punishment or reward stimuli to potentiate or depress KC-to-MBON synapses in specific compartments.
source: Distinct types of DANs react selectively to punishment or reward stimuli to potentiate or depress KC-to-MBON synapses in specific compartments; a process believed to be the neural basis of olfactory associative learning (Aso et al., 2012; Aso and Rubin, 2016; Burke et al., 2012; Das et al., 2014; Galili et al., 2014; Hige et al., 2015a; Huetteroth et al., 2015; Lin et al., 2014b; Liu et al., 2012; Owald et al., 2015; Yamagata et al., 2015).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: The MB is required for innate odor attraction but not repulsion.
source: It was initially reported that the MB is required for innate odor attraction but not repulsion (Wang et al., 2003).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: Recent studies suggest that the MB circuit also regulates innate odor repulsion.
source: However, recent studies suggest that the MB circuit also regulates innate odor repulsion (Bräcker et al., 2013; Lewis et al., 2015; Owald et al., 2015; Perisse et al., 2016; Siju et al., 2014).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: Blocking the MBONs innervating the tips of the horizontal MB lobes impairs a fly's response to aversive odors.
source: Blocking the MBONs innervating the tips of the horizontal MB lobes impairs a fly's response to aversive odors (Lewis et al., 2015; Owald et al., 2015).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: Starvation controls sugar memory expression by modulating odor-evoked responses in MBONs via other neurons in the MB circuit.
source: It has been proposed that starvation controls sugar memory expression by modulating odor-evoked responses in these MBONs via other neurons in the MB circuit (Perisse et al., 2016).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: MBONs respond to CO2 and mediate CO2-induced avoidance behavior in both fed and starved flies.
source: The same MBONs also respond to CO2 and mediate CO2-induced avoidance behavior in both fed and starved flies (Lewis et al., 2015).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: Blocking neurotransmission of the KCs impairs CO2 avoidance only in hungry flies, but not in fed flies.
source: However, blocking neurotransmission of the KCs impairs CO2 avoidance only in hungry flies, but not in fed flies (Bräcker et al., 2013).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: Average yeast food-seeking performance increases linearly with the duration of food deprivation.
source: At the population level, average yeast food-seeking performance increased linearly with the duration of food deprivation, suggesting that hunger regulates food-seeking behavior in a graded manner within a high dynamic range (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the behavioral assay results shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Hunger regulates food-seeking behavior in a graded manner within a high dynamic range.
source: At the population level, average yeast food-seeking performance increased linearly with the duration of food deprivation, suggesting that hunger regulates food-seeking behavior in a graded manner within a high dynamic range (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is inferred from the linear relationship between starvation time and food-seeking performance.

claim: Flies starved for 24 hr did not seek a water-only drop.
source: Flies starved for 24 hr did not seek a water-only drop, confirming that they were attracted to yeast in this assay (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the behavioral assay results shown in Figure 1A.

claim: orco and Ir8a mutant flies could not locate yeast drops.
source: We found that orco and Ir8a mutant flies could not locate yeast drops (Figure 1B), indicating that flies relied on their sense of smell to find the target.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the behavioral assay results shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Flies relied on their sense of smell to find the yeast target.
source: We found that orco and Ir8a mutant flies could not locate yeast drops (Figure 1B), indicating that flies relied on their sense of smell to find the target.
evidence: This is inferred from the inability of olfactory receptor mutants to locate yeast.

claim: Flies use both OR and IR systems to smell yeast odor.
source: This result is consistent with previous findings that flies use both OR and IR systems to smell yeast odor (Gorter et al., 2016; Libert et al., 2007).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature and supported by the current experimental results.

claim: All three major types of KCs—γ, α′β′, and αβ neurons—are important for yeast food-seeking behavior.
source: All three major types of KCs—γ, α′β′, and αβ neurons labeled by MB131B-splitGAL4, MB005B-splitGAL4, and MB008B-splitGAL4, respectively—were found to be important for yeast food-seeking behavior (Figure 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by blocking these neurons with UAS-shits1 and observing impaired food-seeking behavior.

claim: Flies whose KCs were blocked did not show any sign of locomotion defects.
source: Flies whose KCs were blocked did not show any sign of locomotion defects and they performed normally when assayed at the permissive temperature of 23°C (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by behavioral assays at permissive temperature.

claim: Five MBON types—MBON-γ1pedc>αβ, MBON-β2β′2a, MBON-γ2α′1, MBON-α′2, and MBON-α3—are critical for yeast food-seeking behavior in hungry flies.
source: In summary, we have identified five MBON types—MBON-γ1pedc>αβ, MBON-β2β′2a, MBON-γ2α′1, MBON-α′2, and MBON-α3—that are critical for yeast food-seeking behavior in hungry flies.
evidence: This is demonstrated by blocking these MBONs with UAS-shits1 and observing impaired food-seeking behavior.

claim: Not all positive-valence MBONs are required for yeast food-seeking behavior in hungry flies.
source: Interestingly, not all positive-valence MBONs are required for yeast food-seeking behavior in hungry flies (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the screening results of different MBON types.

claim: Only MBON-γ1pedc>αβ and MBON-γ2α′1 encode positive valence and drive approach behavior among the five identified MBONs.
source: Of the five MBONs we identified, only MBON-γ1pedc>αβ and MBON-γ2α′1 encode positive valence and drive approach behavior; the other three MBONs elicit neither approach nor avoidance behavior when optogenetically activated (Aso et al., 2014b).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: All five MBONs required for yeast food-seeking are also important for hungry flies to seek and approach sources of ACV and banana odor.
source: We found that all five MBONs required for yeast food-seeking are also important for hungry flies to seek and approach sources of ACV and banana odor (Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by blocking these MBONs and testing with different food odors.

claim: The three major KC populations are required for ACV- and banana odor-seeking behavior.
source: We also tested the three major KC populations and found that they were also required for ACV- and banana odor-seeking behavior (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by blocking these KCs and testing with different food odors.

claim: The KCs and the five MBONs pathways are generally involved in regulating food odor-seeking behavior in hungry flies.
source: These results indicate that the KCs and the five MBONs pathways we identified using the yeast food-seeking assay are generally involved in regulating food odor-seeking behavior in hungry flies.
evidence: This is inferred from the results with multiple food odors.

claim: All five MBONs showed hunger-dependent changes in their responses to yeast odor.
source: All five MBONs showed hunger-dependent changes in their responses to yeast odor (Figure 5).
evidence: This is demonstrated by in vivo calcium imaging experiments.

claim: Starvation potentiated MBON-γ1pedc>αβ response to yeast odor.
source: Interestingly, starvation modulated the two positive-valence MBONs contrastingly: it potentiated MBON-γ1pedc>αβ and depressed MBON-γ2α′1 (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by in vivo calcium imaging experiments.

claim: Starvation depressed MBON-γ2α′1 response to yeast odor.
source: Interestingly, starvation modulated the two positive-valence MBONs contrastingly: it potentiated MBON-γ1pedc>αβ and depressed MBON-γ2α′1 (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by in vivo calcium imaging experiments.

claim: Hunger-dependent potentiation was observed in MBON-α3.
source: Hunger-dependent potentiation was also observed in MBON-α3 (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by in vivo calcium imaging experiments.

claim: Starvation depressed the response to yeast odor in MBON-β2β′2a and MBON-α′2.
source: In MBON-β2β′2a and MBON-α′2, starvation depressed the neurons' response to yeast odor (Figure 5D and E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by in vivo calcium imaging experiments.

claim: The reduced hunger-dependent odor response for MBON-γ2α′1 and MBON-α′2 was more pronounced for diluted odors.
source: We note that the reduced hunger-dependent odor response for MBON-γ2α′1 and MBON-α′2 was more pronounced for diluted odors (Figure 5B and E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by in vivo calcium imaging experiments with diluted odors.

claim: MBON-γ2α′1 and MBON-α′2 are more sensitive to changes in odor concentration when the fly is starved.
source: Therefore, these neurons are more sensitive to changes in odor concentration (at least for the concentration range that we tested) when the fly is starved.
evidence: This is inferred from the more pronounced response changes to diluted odors.

claim: The starvation-induced modification likely happens at the KC-to-MBON synapses.
source: Since an overall increase or decrease in the responses of KCs to yeast odor should result in a general increase or decrease in odor-evoked responses in the MBONs, the bi-directional tuning suggests that the starvation-induced modification likely happens at the KC-to-MBON synapses.
evidence: This is inferred from the bi-directional modulation of MBON responses and the lack of changes in KC responses.

claim: No difference in food odor-evoked calcium transients was observed in the entire KC population between fed and starved flies.
source: It has been shown that when food odor-evoked calcium transients are measured from the cell bodies of the entire KC population, no difference was observed between fed and starved flies (Beshel and Zhong, 2013).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: Yeast odor-evoked responses in MB lobe compartments innervated by the five food-seeking MBONs did not differ between fed and hungry flies.
source: Consistent with previous findings, the yeast odor-evoked responses in these compartments did not differ between fed and hungry flies (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by calcium imaging experiments in KC compartments.

claim: Ca2+ signal in the α′2 compartment decreased in response to yeast odor in both fed and hungry flies.
source: However, unexpectedly, we found that Ca2+ signal in the α′2 compartment decreased in response to yeast odor in both fed and hungry flies (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by calcium imaging experiments in KC compartments.

claim: Starvation-induced tuning in yeast odor-evoked responses in the five MBONs is not due to changes in the responses of KCs to yeast odor.
source: Overall, our findings and those of others (Beshel and Zhong, 2013) suggest that starvation-induced tuning in yeast odor-evoked responses in the five MBONs is not due to changes in the responses of KCs to yeast odor, supporting that the modulations happen at the KC-to-MBON synapses.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of changes in KC responses and the observed changes in MBON responses.

claim: MBON-γ1pedc>αβ is GABAergic.
source: MBON-γ1pedc>αβ is GABAergic and has been shown to promote appetitive memory expression by inhibiting the activity of MBONs innervating the β′2 zones (Aso et al., 2014a; Perisse et al., 2016).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: MBON-γ1pedc>αβ promotes appetitive memory expression by inhibiting the activity of MBONs innervating the β′2 zones.
source: MBON-γ1pedc>αβ is GABAergic and has been shown to promote appetitive memory expression by inhibiting the activity of MBONs innervating the β′2 zones (Aso et al., 2014a; Perisse et al., 2016).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: RNAi knockdown of GABA biosynthesis in MBON-γ1pedc>αβ resulted in yeast food-seeking defect.
source: RNAi knockdown of GABA biosynthesis in MBON-γ1pedc>αβ using MB112C-splitGAL4 and two independent UAS-GAD-RNAi lines (Koganezawa et al., 2016; Lin et al., 2014a) resulted in the same yeast food-seeking defect caused by blocking the neurons' neurotransmission (Figures 6A and 3A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A), suggesting that MBON-γ1pedc>αβ regulates yeast food-seeking behavior through its release of GABA.
evidence: This is demonstrated by RNAi knockdown experiments.

claim: MBON-γ1pedc>αβ regulates yeast food-seeking behavior through its release of GABA.
source: RNAi knockdown of GABA biosynthesis in MBON-γ1pedc>αβ using MB112C-splitGAL4 and two independent UAS-GAD-RNAi lines (Koganezawa et al., 2016; Lin et al., 2014a) resulted in the same yeast food-seeking defect caused by blocking the neurons' neurotransmission (Figures 6A and 3A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A), suggesting that MBON-γ1pedc>αβ regulates yeast food-seeking behavior through its release of GABA.
evidence: This is inferred from the RNAi knockdown results.

claim: Knockdown of GABA-A receptors in MBON-γ5β′2a and MBON-β′2mp revealed strong impairment of yeast food-seeking behavior in hungry flies.
source: Knockdown of GABA-A receptors using two independent UAS-Rdl-RNAi lines, together with VT1211-GAL4 labeling of MBON-γ5β′2a and MBON-β′2mp, revealed strong impairment of yeast food-seeking behavior in hungry flies (Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by RNAi knockdown experiments.

claim: Blocking neurotransmission of MBON-γ5β′2a and MBON-β′2mp exhibited a significant increase in yeast food-seeking behavior when flies were food-satiated at a restrictive 32°C.
source: Furthermore, when UAS-shits1 was expressed with VT1211-GAL4, the flies exhibited a significant increase in yeast food-seeking behavior when they were food-satiated at a restrictive 32°C, but not at a permissive 23°C (Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by blocking neurotransmission experiments.

claim: The GABAergic pathway is used to control innate hunger-driven food-seeking behavior.
source: These results support the idea that the GABAergic pathway is used to control innate hunger-driven food-seeking behavior.
evidence: This is inferred from the results of GABA and GABA receptor manipulations.

claim: Knockdown of GABA-A receptor in MBON-α1 resulted in decreased yeast food-seeking behavior in hungry flies.
source: Knockdown of the GABA-A receptor with two independent RNAi lines and MB310C-splitGAL4 that specifically labels MBON-α1 resulted in decreased yeast food-seeking behavior in hungry flies (Figure 6D and Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by RNAi knockdown experiments.

claim: Blocking the neurotransmission of MBON-α1 promoted yeast food-seeking behavior in fed flies at a restrictive 32°C.
source: Consistently, blocking the neurotransmission of MBON-α1 with MB310C-splitGAL4 and UAS-shits1 promoted yeast food-seeking behavior in fed flies at a restrictive 32°C, but not at a permissive 23°C (Figure 6E and Figure 6—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by blocking neurotransmission experiments.

claim: When flies are starved, increased GABA release from MBON-γ1pedc>αβ inhibits MBON-γ5β′2a/MBON-β′2mp and MBON-α1 via the GABA-A receptor.
source: These results suggest that when flies are starved, increased GABA release from MBON-γ1pedc>αβ inhibits MBON-γ5β′2a/MBON-β′2mp and MBON-α1 via the GABA-A receptor.
evidence: This is inferred from the results of GABA and GABA receptor manipulations.

claim: Suppression of MBON-γ5β′2a/MBON-β′2mp and MBON-α1 positively biases flies' responses toward yeast odor.
source: In turn, suppression of MBON-γ5β′2a/MBON-β′2mp and MBON-α1 positively biases flies' responses toward yeast odor (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is inferred from the results of GABA and GABA receptor manipulations.

claim: Blockage of PPL1-α3, PAM-β2β′2a, PAM-β′2a, PPL1-α′2α2, and PPL1-γ2α′1 DANs strongly impaired the performances of hungry flies in yeast food-seeking behavior at a restrictive 32°C.
source: Blockage of the neurotransmission of PPL1-α3, PAM-β2β′2a, PAM-β′2a, PPL1-α′2α2, and PPL1-γ2α′1 DANs with UAS-shits1 strongly impaired the performances of hungry flies in yeast food-seeking behavior at a restrictive 32°C, but not at a permissive 23°C (Figure 7A–E and Figure 7—figure supplement 1A–E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by blocking neurotransmission experiments.

claim: Hunger promotes dopamine release in PPL1-α3, PAM-β2β′2a, PAM-β′2a, PPL1-α′2α2, and PPL1-γ2α′1 DANs.
source: These results suggest that the corresponding DANs for MBON-α3, MBON-β2β′2a, MBON-α′2, and MBON-γ2α′1 play important roles in regulating yeast food-seeking behavior and that hunger promotes dopamine release in these DANs.
evidence: This is inferred from the blockage experiments.

claim: PPL1-γ1pedc DANs repress the activity of MBON-γ1pedc>αβ, thereby mediating the hunger control of sugar memory expression.
source: The PPL1-γ1pedc DANs have been shown to repress the activity of MBON-γ1pedc>αβ, thereby mediating the hunger control of sugar memory expression (Perisse et al., 2016).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: Artificial activation of the PPL1-γ1pedc DANs reduced yeast food-seeking behavior in hungry flies at a restrictive 32°C.
source: Consistently, artificial activation of the PPL1-γ1pedc DANs with UAS-TrpA1, a heat-sensitive cation channel transgene (Hamada et al., 2008), reduced yeast food-seeking behavior in hungry flies at a restrictive 32°C (Figure 7F), but not at a permissive 23°C (Figure 7—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by activation experiments.

claim: The fruit fly uses the same PPL1-γ1pedc-to-MBON-γ1pedc>αβ neural pathway to mediate hunger control for both innate and learned food-related olfactory cues.
source: These results indicate that the fruit fly uses the same PPL1-γ1pedc-to-MBON-γ1pedc>αβ neural pathway to mediate hunger control for both innate and learned food-related olfactory cues and that hunger inhibits rather than promotes the release of dopamine by PPL1-γ1pedc DANs.
evidence: This is inferred from the activation and blockage experiments.

claim: Hunger inhibits rather than promotes the release of dopamine by PPL1-γ1pedc DANs.
source: These results indicate that the fruit fly uses the same PPL1-γ1pedc-to-MBON-γ1pedc>αβ neural pathway to mediate hunger control for both innate and learned food-related olfactory cues and that hunger inhibits rather than promotes the release of dopamine by PPL1-γ1pedc DANs.
evidence: This is inferred from the activation and blockage experiments.

claim: Blockage of PPL1-γ1pedc DANs is sufficient to promote sugar memory expression.
source: Blockage of PPL1-γ1pedc DANs is sufficient to promote sugar memory expression (Krashes et al., 2009).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: Blocking the neurotransmission of PPL1-γ1pedc DANs promotes yeast food-seeking behavior in fed flies at a restrictive 32°C.
source: Indeed, blocking the neurotransmission of PPL1-γ1pedc DANs with UAS-shits1 also promotes yeast food-seeking behavior in fed flies at a restrictive 32°C (Figure 7G), but not at a permissive 23°C (Figure 7—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This is demonstrated by blocking neurotransmission experiments.

claim: Artificial activation of PPL1-α3, PAM-β2β′2a, PAM-β′2a, PPL1-α′2α2, and PPL1-γ2α′1 DANs made flies approach yeast food even when they were well fed.
source: Strikingly, in all cases, driving the expression of UAS-TrpA1 with split-GAL4 lines that specifically label these DANs made flies approach yeast food even when they were well fed (Figure 7H–L and Figure 7—figure supplement 1H–L).
evidence: This is demonstrated by activation experiments.

claim: The behavioral phenotypes observed are unlikely due to olfactory learning.
source: However, the behavioral phenotypes we observed here are unlikely due to olfactory learning.
evidence: This is argued based on the mismatch between expected learning effects and observed behaviors, and conditioning experiments.

claim: Pairing odors with artificial activation of PPL1-α3, PPL1-α′2α2, and PPL1-γ2α′1 DANs induces aversive olfactory memories.
source: For PPL1-α3, PPL1-α′2α2, and PPL1-γ2α′1 DANs, pairing the activation of these neurons with odors induces aversive olfactory memories (Aso and Rubin, 2016) but, in our assay, activation of these three DANs promotes rather than inhibits yeast odor-seeking (Figure 7H,I and L).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature and compared with current results.

claim: The six DANs identified might be the main switches the hunger and satiety signals used to tune the innate behavioral response of fruit flies to the smell of food.
source: These results and the anatomy of the MB circuits indicate that the six DANs we have identified might be the main switches the hunger and satiety signals used to tune the innate behavioral response of fruit flies to the smell of food.
evidence: This is inferred from the results of DAN manipulations and conditioning experiments.

claim: DAMB and Dop2R mutant flies exhibited strong yeast food-seeking defects.
source: The DAMB and Dop2R mutant flies exhibited strong yeast food-seeking defects, whereas the DopR1 and DopEcR mutant flies performed normally (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by behavioral assays with dopamine receptor mutants.

claim: Knockdown of DAMB in all the KCs severely compromised yeast food-seeking behavior in hungry flies.
source: In stark contrast, knockdown of DAMB in all the KCs with two independent RNAi lines and MB010B-splitGAL4 severely compromised yeast food-seeking behavior in hungry flies (Figure 8B and Figure 8-figure supplement 1A), suggesting that the DANs regulate the response of flies to yeast food by pre-synaptically modulating KC-to-MBON connectivity via the DAMB receptor.
evidence: This is demonstrated by RNAi knockdown experiments.

claim: The DANs regulate the response of flies to yeast food by pre-synaptically modulating KC-to-MBON connectivity via the DAMB receptor.
source: In stark contrast, knockdown of DAMB in all the KCs with two independent RNAi lines and MB010B-splitGAL4 severely compromised yeast food-seeking behavior in hungry flies (Figure 8B and Figure 8-figure supplement 1A), suggesting that the DANs regulate the response of flies to yeast food by pre-synaptically modulating KC-to-MBON connectivity via the DAMB receptor.
evidence: This is inferred from the RNAi knockdown results.

claim: DAMB is strongly expressed in all KC types.
source: This is not surprising because DAMB is strongly expressed in all KC types (Han et al., 1996).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: DAMB in the MBONs is also required for yeast food-seeking behavior.
source: However, we found that DAMB in the MBONs is also required for yeast food-seeking behavior.
evidence: This is demonstrated by RNAi knockdown experiments in MBONs.

claim: Knockdown of DAMB in MBON-β2β′2a, MBON-γ2α′1, and MBON-α3 significantly impaired yeast food-seeking behavior in hungry flies.
source: Knockdown of DAMB in MBON-β2β′2a, MBON-γ2α′1, and MBON-α3 with two independent RNAi lines significantly impaired yeast food-seeking behavior in hungry flies (Figure 8C–E and Figure 8—figure supplement 1B–D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by RNAi knockdown experiments.

claim: Knockdown of DAMB in MBON-γ1pedc>αβ promoted yeast food-seeking behavior in fed flies.
source: Furthermore, knockdown of DAMB in MBON-1pedc>αβ with two independent RNAi lines promoted yeast food-seeking behavior in fed flies (Figure 8F and Figure 8—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by RNAi knockdown experiments.

claim: DAMB knockdown in MBON-α′2 had no detectable effect on yeast food-seeking behavior in hungry flies.
source: DAMB knockdown in MBON-α′2 had no detectable effect on yeast food-seeking behavior in hungry flies (Figure 8G and Figure 8—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by RNAi knockdown experiments.

claim: The DANs modulate the MB circuit both pre- and post-synaptically via the DAMB receptor to control the behavioral response of flies to yeast food.
source: Taken together, these data suggest that the DANs modulate the MB circuit both pre- and post-synaptically via the DAMB receptor to control the behavioral response of flies to yeast food.
evidence: This is inferred from the RNAi knockdown results in both KCs and MBONs.

claim: Starvation decreased the yeast odor-evoked calcium transient in PPL1-γ1pedc DANs.
source: Interestingly, we found that starvation decreased the yeast odor-evoked calcium transient in PPL1-γ1pedc DANs but increased it in PPL1-α3 DANs, consistent with our behavioral data (Figure 9A and B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by in vivo calcium imaging experiments.

claim: Starvation increased the yeast odor-evoked calcium transient in PPL1-α3 DANs.
source: Interestingly, we found that starvation decreased the yeast odor-evoked calcium transient in PPL1-γ1pedc DANs but increased it in PPL1-α3 DANs, consistent with our behavioral data (Figure 9A and B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by in vivo calcium imaging experiments.

claim: No starvation-induced change in odor-evoked responses was detected in PAM-β2β′2a and PPL1-α′2α2 DANs.
source: However, we did not detect starvation-induced change in odor-evoked responses of PAM-β2β′2a and PPL1-α′2α2 DANs (Figure 9C and D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by in vivo calcium imaging experiments.

claim: Some DANs receive direct inputs from the KCs.
source: Recent studies have found that some DANs receive direct inputs from the KCs (Cervantes-Sandoval et al., 2017; Takemura et al., 2017).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: PPL1-γ1pedc and MBON-γ1pedc>αβ innervate the same compartment in the MB lobes, but their yeast odor-evoked responses are contrastingly modulated by starvation.
source: It is noteworthy that PPL1-γ1pedc and MBON-γ1pedc>αβ innervate the same compartment in the MB lobes, but their yeast odor-evoked responses are contrastingly modulated by starvation (Figures 5A and 9A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparing calcium imaging results.

claim: The starvation-induced modulations observed are not due to changes in circuits upstream of the KCs.
source: This supports our notion that the starvation-induced modulations we observed are not due to changes in circuits upstream of the KCs.
evidence: This is inferred from the contrasting modulation of PPL1-γ1pedc and MBON-γ1pedc>αβ.

claim: The mean intensity of DSyd-1-GFP in PPL1-γ2α′1, PAM-β2β′2a, and PPL1-α′2α2 DANs is statistically higher in hungry flies.
source: Therefore, we expressed an active zone marker DSyd-1-GFP (Owald et al., 2010) in our identified DANs and found that the mean intensity of DSyd-1-GFP in PPL1-γ2α′1, PAM-β2β′2a, and PPL1-α′2α2 DANs is statistically higher in hungry flies (Figure 9—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence staining and imaging.

claim: The mean intensity of the DenMark signals in PPL1-γ2α′1, PAM-β2β′2a, and PPL1-α′2α2 DANs did not differ between fed and hungry flies.
source: Importantly, the mean intensity of the DenMark signals in these DANs did not differ between fed and hungry flies (Figure 9—figure supplement 1A–C), suggesting that the increase of DSyd-1-GFP signal is not due to higher GAL4 activity or other non-specific effects caused by starvation.
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence staining and imaging.

claim: Starvation may increase the density or size of the active zones in PPL1-γ2α′1, PAM-β2β′2a, and PPL1-α′2α2 DANs, elevating their dopamine release in hungry flies.
source: These results indicate that starvation may increase the density or size of the active zones in PPL1-γ2α′1, PAM-β2β′2a, and PPL1-α′2α2 DANs, elevating their dopamine release in hungry flies.
evidence: This is inferred from the increased DSyd-1-GFP signal.

claim: No starvation-induced change in DSyd-1-GFP signal was detected in PPL1-γ1pedc or PPL1-α3 DANs.
source: Moreover, we did not detect starvation-induced change in DSyd-1-GFP signal in PPL1-γ1pedc or PPL1-α3 DANs (Figure 9—figure supplement 1D and E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence staining and imaging.

claim: Serotonin is a general hunger signal that affects a wide range of feeding-related behaviors in the fly.
source: A recent study demonstrated that serotonin is a general hunger signal that affects a wide range of feeding-related behaviors in the fly (Albin et al., 2015).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: Blocking serotoninergic neurons resulted in a strong yeast food-seeking defect in hungry flies at a restrictive 32°C.
source: To examine whether serotonin also regulates hunger-evoked yeast food-seeking behavior, we first used R50H05-GAL4 (Albin et al., 2015) and UAS-shits1 to block serotoninergic neurons in hungry flies. We observed a strong yeast food-seeking defect in these flies at a restrictive 32°C, but not at a permissive 23°C (Figure 10A and Figure 10—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by blocking neurotransmission experiments.

claim: Artificial activation of the R50H05-positive serotoninergic neurons promoted yeast food-seeking behavior in fed flies at 32°C.
source: Conversely, artificial activation of the R50H05-positive serotoninergic neurons with UAS-TrpA1 promoted yeast food-seeking behavior in fed flies at 32°C, but not at 23°C (Figure 10B and Figure 10—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by activation experiments.

claim: Serotonin receptors in PPL1-γ2α′1 and PPL1-γ1pedc DANs are critical for yeast food-seeking behavior in hungry flies.
source: We found that serotonin receptors in PPL1-γ2α′1 and PPL1-γ1pedc DANs are critical for yeast food-seeking behavior in hungry flies (Figure 10C–F), suggesting that hunger-evoked serotonin release may control the response of flies to the smell of yeast food through these two DANs.
evidence: This is demonstrated by RNAi knockdown experiments of serotonin receptors.

claim: Hunger-evoked serotonin release may control the response of flies to the smell of yeast food through PPL1-γ2α′1 and PPL1-γ1pedc DANs.
source: We found that serotonin receptors in PPL1-γ2α′1 and PPL1-γ1pedc DANs are critical for yeast food-seeking behavior in hungry flies (Figure 10C–F), suggesting that hunger-evoked serotonin release may control the response of flies to the smell of yeast food through these two DANs.
evidence: This is inferred from the RNAi knockdown results.

claim: PPL1-γ2α′1 and PPL1-γ1pedc DANs are regulated by different serotonin receptors.
source: Interestingly, the two DAN types are regulated by different serotonin receptors.
evidence: This is demonstrated by RNAi knockdown experiments of different serotonin receptors.

claim: Knockdown of 5HT1B receptors in PPL1-γ2α′1 DANs impaired yeast food-seeking behavior.
source: Knockdown of 5HT1B receptors in PPL1-γ2α′1 DANs with two independent RNAi lines impaired yeast food-seeking behavior (Figure 10C, Figure 10—figure supplement 3A), but no significant defect was detected when the same receptor was knocked down in PPL1-γ1pedc DANs (Figure 10D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by RNAi knockdown experiments.

claim: Knockdown of 5HT2A receptors in PPL1-γ1pedc DANs strongly impaired yeast food-seeking behavior.
source: In contrast, no phenotypic deficiency was observed when 5HT2A receptors were knocked down in PPL-γ2α′1 DANs (Figure 10E), whereas knockdown of 5HT2A receptors with two independent RNAi lines in the PPL1-γ1pedc DANs strongly impaired yeast food-seeking behavior (Figure 10F and Figure 10—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by RNAi knockdown experiments.

claim: Differential usage of serotonin receptors may potentially explain how starvation activates PPL1-γ2α′1 DANs but inhibits PPL1-γ1pedc DANs.
source: Differential usage of these serotonin receptors may potentially explain how starvation activates PPL1-γ2α′1 DANs but inhibits PPL1-γ1pedc DANs.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential receptor usage and known receptor signaling properties.

claim: Different 5HT receptors have opposing effects on cAMP signaling when expressed in mammalian cells.
source: In support of this idea, different 5HT receptors have been shown to have opposing effects on cAMP signaling when expressed in mammalian cells (Saudou et al., 1992).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: Knockdown of NPFR in PPL1-γ1pedc DANs resulted in diminished yeast-seeking performances of hungry flies.
source: NPF and sNPF are hunger-evoked neuropeptides, and NPF is suggested to inhibit the activity of PPL1-γ1pedc when flies are hungry (Krashes et al., 2009). Consistently, when NPF receptors (NPFR) were knocked down with two independent RNAi lines in PPL1-γ1pedc DANs, the yeast-seeking performances of hungry flies diminished significantly (Figure 11A and Figure 11—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by RNAi knockdown experiments.

claim: Knockdown of sNPFR in PPL1-γ1pedc DANs impaired yeast food-seeking behavior.
source: In addition, we found that knockdown of sNPF receptors (sNPFR) with two independent RNAi lines in PPL1-γ1pedc DANs impaired yeast food-seeking behavior (Figure 11B and Figure 11—figure supplement 1B), suggesting that serotonin, NPF, and sNPF work together to suppress PPL1-γ1pedc DANs in hungry flies.
evidence: This is demonstrated by RNAi knockdown experiments.

claim: Serotonin, NPF, and sNPF work together to suppress PPL1-γ1pedc DANs in hungry flies.
source: In addition, we found that knockdown of sNPF receptors (sNPFR) with two independent RNAi lines in PPL1-γ1pedc DANs impaired yeast food-seeking behavior (Figure 11B and Figure 11—figure supplement 1B), suggesting that serotonin, NPF, and sNPF work together to suppress PPL1-γ1pedc DANs in hungry flies.
evidence: This is inferred from the RNAi knockdown results.

claim: Knockdown of NPFR in PAM-β′2a, PPL1-α3 and PAM-β2β′2a DANs impaired yeast food-seeking behavior in hungry flies.
source: Knockdown of NPFR in PAM-β′2a, PPL1-α3 and PAM-β2β′2a DANs, but not the other two DAN types, impaired yeast food-seeking behavior in hungry flies (Figure 11C,E,G,I and K; Figure 11—figure supplement 1H,K and M).
evidence: This is demonstrated by RNAi knockdown experiments.

claim: Knockdown of sNPFR in all but PPL1-α′2α2 DANs reduced the yeast food-seeking behavior of hungry flies.
source: In contrast, knockdown of sNPFR in all but PPL1-α′2α2 DANs reduced the yeast food-seeking behavior of hungry flies (Figure 11D,F,H,J and L; Figure 11—figure supplement 1C,I,L and N).
evidence: This is demonstrated by RNAi knockdown experiments.

claim: DANs are regulated by multiple hunger signals in a cell-type-specific manner.
source: These results argue that these DANs are regulated by multiple hunger signals in a cell-type-specific manner.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential effects of NPFR and sNPFR knockdown in different DANs.

claim: RNAi knockdown of Insulin receptor (dInR) in PAM-β′2a, PPL1-α′2α2, and PPL1-γ2α′1 DANs promoted yeast food-seeking behavior in fed flies.
source: RNAi knockdown of Insulin receptor (dInR) in PAM-β′2a, PPL1-α′2α2, and PPL1-γ2α′1 DANs promoted yeast food-seeking behavior in fed flies (Figure 11O,Q and S; Figure 11—figure supplement 1D,F and J), whereas no altered phenotype was observed when dInR was knocked down in PPL1-α3, PAM-β2β′2a, and PPL1-γ1pedc DANs (Figure 11M,U and W).
evidence: This is demonstrated by RNAi knockdown experiments.

claim: Flies expressing DAR1 RNAi in PPL1-γ2α′1, PPL1-α′2α2, and PAM-β2β′2a DANs exhibited increased food-seeking behavior when they were food-satiated.
source: Flies expressing two independent DAR1 RNAi (Yamagata et al., 2016) in PPL1-γ2α′1, PPL1-α′2α2, and PAM-β2β′2a DANs exhibited increased food-seeking behavior when they were food-satiated (Figure 11P,R and X; Figure 11—figure supplement 1E,G and O).
evidence: This is demonstrated by RNAi knockdown experiments.

claim: No phenotypic difference was detected when DAR1 was knocked down in PPL1-α3, PAM-β′2a, and PPL1-γ1pedc DANs.
source: No phenotypic difference was detected when DAR1 was knocked down in PPL1-α3, PAM-β′2a, and PPL1-γ1pedc DANs (Figure 11N,T and V).
evidence: This is demonstrated by RNAi knockdown experiments.

claim: The RNAi knockdown data suggest potential rich hunger and satiety inputs to the MB circuits that control the innate behavioral response of flies to the smell of yeast food.
source: Overall, our RNAi knockdown data suggest potential rich hunger and satiety inputs to the MB circuits that control the innate behavioral response of flies to the smell of yeast food (Figure 12).
evidence: This is inferred from the comprehensive RNAi knockdown results.

claim: The MB plays an essential role in controlling food-seeking behavior.
source: In this study, we show that the MB plays an essential role in controlling food-seeking behavior.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study based on all the experimental findings.

claim: Flies approach yeast food only when they are hungry.
source: Flies approach yeast food only when they are hungry.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the behavioral assays showing increased food-seeking with starvation.

claim: The MB may receive remarkably rich inputs of hunger and satiety signals.
source: An unexpected finding of our study is that the MB may receive remarkably rich inputs of hunger and satiety signals.
evidence: This is inferred from the RNAi knockdown experiments showing differential regulation of DANs by multiple signals.

claim: PPL1-γ1pedc DANs are regulated by NPF.
source: It has previously been shown that PPL1-γ1pedc DANs are regulated by NPF (Krashes et al., 2009).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: The six DAN types regulating food-seeking behavior are differentially modulated by combinations of hunger and satiety signals.
source: Here, we tested two satiety signals (insulin and AstA) and three hunger signals (serotonin, sNPF, and NPF), and found that the six DAN types regulating food-seeking behavior are differentially modulated by combinations of these signals.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the RNAi knockdown experiments.

claim: PPL1-γ1pedc and PPL1-α3 DANs are regulated exclusively by hunger signals.
source: PPL1-γ1pedc and PPL1-α3 DANs are regulated exclusively by hunger signals, whereas PPL1-α′2α2 DANs only receive satiety signals.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the RNAi knockdown experiments.

claim: PPL1-α′2α2 DANs only receive satiety signals.
source: PPL1-γ1pedc and PPL1-α3 DANs are regulated exclusively by hunger signals, whereas PPL1-α′2α2 DANs only receive satiety signals.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the RNAi knockdown experiments.

claim: Three DAN types (PPL1-γ2α′1, PAM-β′2a, PAM-β2β′2a) are regulated by both hunger and satiety signals.
source: The other three DAN types are regulated by both signals.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the RNAi knockdown experiments.

claim: Hunger gates memory formation.
source: Indeed, in addition to controlling appetitive memory expression (Krashes et al., 2009; Perisse et al., 2016), hunger also gates memory formation (Hirano et al., 2013; Huetteroth et al., 2015; Musso et al., 2015; Plaçais et al., 2017).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: Feeding flies nutritious sugar after olfactory learning changes the activity of PPL1-γ1pedc DANs and this change upregulates energy metabolism in the MB to promote long-term memory consolidation.
source: In particular, feeding flies nutritious sugar after olfactory learning changes the activity of PPL1-γ1pedc DANs and this change upregulates energy metabolism in the MB to promote long-term memory consolidation (Musso et al., 2015; Plaçais et al., 2017).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: Nutritious sugar feeding immediately suppresses the PAM-γ3 DANs via the AstA signaling pathway, and this suppression provides a positive reinforcing signal for the formation of sugar-odor associative memory.
source: Nutritious sugar feeding has also been shown to immediately suppress the PAM-γ3 DANs via the AstA signaling pathway, and this suppression provides a positive reinforcing signal for the formation of sugar-odor associative memory (Yamagata et al., 2016).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: Starvation recruits the MB for CO2 avoidance behavior.
source: Furthermore, starvation recruits the MB for CO2 avoidance behavior (Bräcker et al., 2013).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: The MB circuit has been shown to be involved in thirst-driven water-seeking.
source: The MB circuit has been shown to be involved in thirst-driven water-seeking (Lin et al., 2014b), sleep (Joiner et al., 2006; Pitman et al., 2006), decision-making (DasGupta et al., 2014), and temperature preference behavior (Bang et al., 2011; Hong et al., 2008; Shih et al., 2015).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: The MB may serve as an integration center for hunger to interact with other motivations, giving rise to hierarchical behaviors.
source: Given the broad influence of hunger and satiety on the MB-innervating DANs, the MB may serve as an integration center for hunger to interact with other motivations, giving rise to hierarchical behaviors.
evidence: This is inferred from the broad influence of hunger and satiety on DANs and the MB's involvement in multiple behaviors.

claim: Hunger tunes the response of MBONs to yeast odor in a cell-type-specific manner.
source: Our study reveals that hunger tunes the response of MBONs to yeast odor in a cell-type-specific manner.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the calcium imaging experiments showing different modulation patterns in different MBONs.

claim: The level of odor-evoked response might be critical in some MBONs.
source: These unexpected results suggest that the level of odor-evoked response might be critical in some MBONs.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that starvation depresses responses in some MBONs required for food-seeking.

claim: A putative circuit mechanism is proposed where MBONs connect to two downstream neurons with different connectivity strength, and the weakly connected downstream neuron inhibits the strongly connected one.
source: We propose a putative circuit mechanism to explain this phenomenon (Figure 12—figure supplement 1). In this putative configuration, MBONs like MBON-β2β′2a, MBON-α′2, and MBON-γ2α′1 connect to two downstream neurons with different connectivity strength, and the weakly connected downstream neuron (neuron B) inhibits the strongly connected one (neuron A).
evidence: This is a hypothetical model proposed to explain the observed data.

claim: A similar activity level-dependent mechanism has been observed in courtship-promoting P1 interneurons in the fly.
source: A similar activity level-dependent mechanism has been observed in courtship-promoting P1 interneurons in the fly (Hoopfer et al., 2015).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: Low-frequency activation of P1 neurons evokes aggression, whereas high-frequency activation of the same neurons inhibits aggression but promotes wing extension.
source: Low-frequency activation of P1 neurons evokes aggression, whereas high-frequency activation of the same neurons inhibits aggression but promotes wing extension.
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: Hunger-induced modulation appears to occur both pre- and post-synaptically through DAMB receptors.
source: Hunger-induced modulation appears to occur both pre- and post-synaptically through DAMB receptors.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the RNAi knockdown experiments in both KCs and MBONs.

claim: DAMB is mainly distributed in axonal processes, but is absent from dendrites.
source: DAMB is highly expressed in all KCs, and immunostaining results have showed that DAMB is mainly distributed in axonal processes, but is absent from dendrites (Han et al., 1996).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: DAMB might also function in the dendrites of the MBONs.
source: However, our data suggest that DAMB might also function in the dendrites of the MBONs.
evidence: This is inferred from the RNAi knockdown results in MBONs.

claim: DAMB is required in MBON-α′3 to allow flies to become accustomed to novel odors.
source: Consistent with this possibility, a recent study found that DAMB is required in MBON-α′3 to allow flies to become accustomed to novel odors (Hattori et al., 2017).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: DopR1 is critical for the acquisition of olfactory memories.
source: DopR1 has been shown to be critical for the acquisition of olfactory memories (Kim et al., 2007; Qin et al., 2012), whereas DAMB is mainly required for memory maintenance (Berry et al., 2012; Musso et al., 2015; Plaçais et al., 2017).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: DAMB is mainly required for memory maintenance.
source: DopR1 has been shown to be critical for the acquisition of olfactory memories (Kim et al., 2007; Qin et al., 2012), whereas DAMB is mainly required for memory maintenance (Berry et al., 2012; Musso et al., 2015; Plaçais et al., 2017).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: An attractive hypothesis is that phasic dopamine release evoked by rewards or punishments during learning activates DopR1, and tonic (or spontaneous) dopamine release mainly engages DAMB.
source: An attractive hypothesis is that phasic dopamine release evoked by rewards or punishments during learning activates DopR1, and tonic (or spontaneous) dopamine release mainly engages DAMB (Berry and Davis, 2014; Ichinose et al., 2017).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature as a hypothesis.

claim: The lack of stereotypic connectivity between olfactory inputs and the KCs, together with the reinforcing DANs and the valence-encoding MBONs, make the MB an ideal center for olfactory learning.
source: The lack of stereotypic connectivity between olfactory inputs and the KCs, together with the reinforcing DANs and the valence-encoding MBONs, make the MB an ideal center for olfactory learning (Owald and Waddell, 2015).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: Learning activates distinct reinforcing DANs that skew the MBON outputs by changing the connectivity of specific KC-to-MBON synapses.
source: It has been suggested that a given odor drives a collection of balanced MBON outputs in naive flies, and learning activates distinct reinforcing DANs that skew the outputs by changing the connectivity of specific KC-to-MBON synapses (Aso et al., 2014b; Owald and Waddell, 2015).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: Learning only modifies the output synapses of the KCs that are activated near to when reinforcement signals are triggered.
source: Although each MBON and DAN is in contact with a large number of KCs wherein odors are sparsely coded, learning only modifies the output synapses of the KCs that are activated near to when reinforcement signals are triggered.
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: Learning only skews the MBON outputs driven by trained odors.
source: Therefore, learning only skews the MBON outputs driven by trained odors.
evidence: This is inferred from the mechanism of learning described.

claim: Odor specificity is more difficult to achieve in MB-mediated motivated behavior.
source: Such odor specificity is more difficult to achieve in MB-mediated motivated behavior.
evidence: This is inferred from the difference between learning and hunger-driven behavior.

claim: Hunger seems to regulate DAN activity and tip the balance of MBON outputs independently of olfactory inputs.
source: Hunger seems to regulate DAN activity and tip the balance of MBON outputs independently of olfactory inputs.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental results showing hunger modulation of DANs.

claim: The MB is dispensable for CO2 avoidance in food-satiated flies but, when flies are starved, blockage of the KCs decreases CO2 avoidance.
source: It has been shown that the MB is dispensable for CO2 avoidance in food-satiated flies but, when flies are starved, blockage of the KCs decreases CO2 avoidance (Bräcker et al., 2013).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: Starvation seems to change the CO2-driven MBON output valence from nil to negative.
source: Therefore, starvation in this scenario seems to change the CO2-driven MBON output valence from nil to negative.
evidence: This is inferred from the cited literature.

claim: MBONs are generally broadly tuned to odors, but they do encode some odor specificity.
source: A comprehensive study on odor tuning in MBONs suggests that although MBONs are generally broadly tuned to odors, they do encode some odor specificity.
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: Odor groups of opposing valence are well separated in the MBON coding space.
source: In particular, odor groups of opposing valence are well separated in the MBON coding space (Hige et al., 2015b).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.
